notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0022.stoa045.opp-la: Ch. I: 'unione recunda' is evidently corrupt; read as 'fecunda' (fruitful), possibly 'jucunda' (delightful). 'condilril' read as 'conditoris' (of the Creator). Ch. III: the list of categories names 'neither born nor made' twice (for the Father and for the Spirit) as the text stands; translated as given. The Psalm reference is printed as 'LXVI, 8' and Romans as 'XI, 55' (for 36). Ch. II: the closing sentence on Arius lacks a main clause in the text as printed, and is left incomplete.

Ch. V: 'tam filum' is evidently corrupt; rendered as 'tam fixum' ('so fixed'). The biblical reference 'Rom. 8:15' is printed after the list of attributes but belongs with 'Spirit of adoption'. Ch. VI: the sentence 'tenebras et angustias ac pusillanimitatem cordis et sua nos luce illuminans' lacks a main verb for 'darkness... faintness of heart'; a verb such as 'expellit' seems to have dropped out, supplied as '[dispels]'. In the closing list, the final sentence's grammar is loose: 'Spiritus' stands alongside the titles of the Son, while the text says they all point to the person of the Son; translated as it stands.

Ch. VII: the sentence on Paul's 'goad of the flesh' (quem postea ... idcirco cum dixit datum sibi) is garbled in the text; translated by sense. Ch. VIII: 'vacasse mensam' is uncertain; read as 'vacasse mensae' (gave themselves to a table). Ch. IX: 'lim pre certo neverimus' read as 'dum pro certo noverimus'; 'animam quia obsides' read as 'quia animam ac obsides'. Several biblical references in the edition are mis-scanned or inaccurate (e.g. Baruch 3:36 for 3:38, the 'man in sorrow' attributed to Baruch rather than Isa. 53:3); corrected where evident.

Line 10: 'Ergo fides non sit in hominum sapientia, et hæresis non est' is elliptical; rendered literally. The Isaiah vision is cited as Isa. VI, 3 in the edition (actually 6:2). The final scriptural reference lists Ecclesiasticus/Sirach passages under 'Eccl.'; the honey saying is Prov. 25:27. Line 11: 'Deus Pater a propria generatio est' appears corrupt; read as 'propria generatione' (Father by his own generation). 'cibi' read as 'sibi'.

Ch. XII: 'Sicut ergo Pater sine princinio, f lia et Spi- filum sanctumat Filiumhabet' is badly garbled; read as 'ita et Spiritum sanctum et Filium habet sine principio coaeternum'. Ch. XIII: 'Anima ergo in secreta rationabili ante Verbum Dei capiente' seems corrupt; translated as if 'in secreto rationabili', with the soul receiving the Word first. 'qui se facturam per superbiam cognoscens' is awkward; taken as 'knowing himself to be a creature, [yet] through pride…'. Scripture references are reproduced as printed, several of them inaccurate (e.g. Ps. 1:14, Luke 10:19 for 'I, t9').

Line 14: 'Hæc porta DQlijini' read as 'Domini'; 'de portis morus' as 'mortis'. The verse cited as Ps. 126:5 is quoted out of order in the edition. The Pauline citation is 1 Cor. 1:18, not 1:24–25 as printed. Line 15: 'ut crede- fumus nus' is garbled; read as 'ut credere possimus nos'. Line 16: 'homo, rei, et Deus' read as 'homo, rex, et Deus' (man, king and God). 'terni stratores diaboli': 'stratores' (grooms, attendants, or road-layers) is uncertain in sense here; possibly a corruption. 'qui bona Pol ducet ct c delectatur' is corrupt (perhaps 'qui bona producit et delectatur'); marked [...]. The final sentence ('affliction autem corporis') may be incomplete or mispunctuated.

Ch. XVIII: the scan reads 'teW tIIr' in the list of the soul's afflictions; taken as 'contristatur' ('is saddened') from the parallel list that follows. The quotation 'Qui format spiritum hominis in eo', attributed to Isaiah, is Zech. 12:1. The bronze/iron threat cited under Lev. 26:19 matches Deut. 28:23 more closely. The edition's reference 'Gen. II, 23' in ch. XVII is for the woman taken from Adam's side (Gen. 2:21–22).

21: 'sus inentibus vero pœnam ignsi sse videntur' is garbled; read as 'sustinentibus vero poenam ignis esse videatur' ('to those undergoing punishment he seems to be fire'). The citation 'Hebr. XII, 23' should be 12:29. 22: 'Sepultura ejus sublata est' appears to be Isa. 57:2 (LXX); Moses and Elijah at the Transfiguration are Matt. 17:3. 24: 'Cui ergo' at 'Then, therefore, there will be neither...' read as 'Tunc ergo'; text uncertain. 25: a printed footnote ('h Eadem Rom. edit., et in mensuram plenitudinis ejus resurgemus', a variant from the Roman edition for 'we shall rise into the perfect man' in ch. 24) has intruded into the text and is omitted. The final reference to Tertullian 'cap. 55' is probably ch. 35.

Ch. XXVI: 'nubis ... carnia ... mule' read as 'nobis ... carnis ... mole'; 'in simplicis gloria' as 'in simplici gloria'. Ch. XXVII: 'nec cunt errat, ignorat' is corrupt; translated tentatively as 'qui nescit, errat'. 'teneris Hiericuntinus' is corrupt; taken as the wounded man of Jericho. 'per miscientis gratiam' read as 'misericordis'. A line seems lost after 'utuntur vesti-' (probably 'vestimentis, sed'), marked [...]. Ch. XXIX: 'Lunceus' read as Lynceus; 'pendulo ... itrtessu' as 'pendulo incessu'. Several of the edition's bracketed references appear garbled in the scan and have been corrected where evident.

Ch. 30: the scriptural reference '(Joan. XX, 16)' is attached to words from Luke 24:31; kept as printed. Ch. 31: the verse cited as Ps. 108:4 does not match the usual Latin psalm text; translated as the tract gives it. 'Vaginam' (sheath) is taken as a figure for the body. Ch. 33: 'aut in istis factis pejeraret' read as 'factus'; 'quidquid hæredum' read as 'hæredibus'; 'bonestatem' read as 'honestatem'.

Ch. 34: 'suas salutis obsidem' read as 'suae salutis'; the subject of 'habet' (the flesh) and the referent of 'verum et pacificum' are not clear. 'naturali One discindens atque succindens' read, after Tertullian De resurr. 13, as 'naturali fine decedens atque succedens'. 'Florebunt velut phoenix' reflects Ps. 91(92):13, where Greek 'phoinix' means 'palm'. 'Usque ad nubes et ignem' presumably means the fiery region of the upper air. Ch. 35: the quotation of John 5:29 seems to have lost a clause: it should read 'those who have done good into the resurrection of life, those who have done evil into the resurrection of judgment'. The reference 'Prov. 25:3' is corrected to 25:20 and 'Matt. 22:15' to 22:13. 'Musicorum' is taken as 'musical instruments'.

nodes.text: ON THE TRINITY, OTHERWISE A TREATISE ON THE CREED OF THE APOSTLES.

CHAPTER ONE. Therefore let no one of sound mind think that almighty God, who is Trinity and is spirit, is some visible or tangible body; but let him understand [him to be] a simple, rational and invisible nature, one not held together by any joining at all, nor to which anything seems to be added from outside or from elsewhere: whom no substance, no creature, no dominion ever precedes. The source, then, and origin of all powers and of all visible and invisible creatures, that is, of heavenly and earthly things, is the holy and inseparable Trinity of the Creator, which takes into itself nothing external, lest it should seem to be bounded, or be found to be in need of anything; but it is always fruitful in a pure, single-formed and mystical union, so to speak. For so great is the inseparable and unconfused essence of unity in the three that the holy Trinity is seen to do nothing outside itself: in this holy and inseparable Trinity is true eternity, unchangeable truth, and eternal and perfect love. And therefore God is more truly thought than spoken of, because he is always incomprehensible. So God almighty, who has neither sex, nor age, nor defined bodily limbs, wished himself to be proclaimed in this way, most excellently, most clearly and most magnificently. Eternity, then, is in the Father, beauty in the Image, enjoyment in the Gift (Augustine, On the Trinity VI.10; Hilary, On the Trinity II): and these three are one God; yet not consisting in the singleness of one person, but in the essence of one Trinity. So there is one who loves him who is from him, and one who loves him from whom he is, and the love itself is the one same [love] of both, that is, the Holy Spirit. And yet these three, as has been said, are one God: good, true, just, light, life, truth, spirit and love. God, then, because he is eternal and the author of all things, cannot be understood as composite, lest the things of which he is thought to be composed should be prior to God. So the whole creation, which is not what he is, none made but he himself. Therefore none can be called eternal except him who lacks beginning and end, that is, God the Father, who has the Word and the Spirit co-eternal and co-almighty with himself. This understanding clearly proves that the substance of the Son and of the Holy Spirit exists before all creation and outside all times, and remains always with [its] origin in God the Father. The Holy Spirit, then, is not begotten, but is the sweetness, holiness and eternity of the begetter and the begotten. For though the Father is Spirit and the Son is Spirit, and the Father is holy and the Son is holy, yet it is properly of the Spirit that 'Holy Spirit' is said. Because, then, he is co-eternal and common to both, he is called that which both are.

CHAPTER II. With what rashness and misfortune the Arians must now be judged, who say, 'There was a time when the Son was not', the reader understands. For could there ever have been a time when the Father was without life, without wisdom, without power, without the Word, which is Christ? Far from it; since the Father himself plainly declares, saying: My heart has uttered a good Word (Ps. 44:2). Confirming this, blessed John says: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. This was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made (John 1:1-3). Whatever, then, is incorporeal and invisible cannot be separated by difference of places. For if our word, or power, or wisdom cannot be separated from us except when we depart from the body, how could these be separated from the immortal and almighty God, who made all things out of nothing through his Word? For whose Father will he be, according to the impious heretics, if the nature of the Son is separated from him? And again, whose Son will the Son be, if his origin is not referred to the Father, so that there is he who begot and he who was begotten from him? The Father, then, who is the origin of deity and goodness, is rightly understood and perceived both in the Son and in the Holy Spirit: in the one, that is, in the Son, as Word, power and wisdom; in the other, as the Spirit proceeding from him. So it is right and catholic that we both confess one God according to the truth of substance, and perceive the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit each in his own subsistence. The divinity of the holy Trinity, then, is to be believed to be without any end, and difficult even for the mind itself to perceive. And this alone is what we grasp of it: that it cannot be grasped. There is, then, one deity in three, and there are three in whom the deity is. So there is no confusion in the unity, nor division in the divinity. And therefore both the mingling of the foolish Sabellius and the separating of the impious Arius are equally to be rejected: for they put forward things contrary to each other, but equally impious. For Sabellius, while he thinks all [three] are [mere] names, makes each one out to be nothing, since indeed what is ceases to be when it is poured over into the other, [namely] that which is said to be the being of each; Arius, however, while he impiously asserts that the Son is a creature of the Father, and the Holy Spirit a creature of the Son.

CHAPTER III. But with these impieties cast out and scorned, for us, as blessed Paul the apostle says: There is one God the Father, from whom are all things; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things; and one Holy Spirit, in whom are all things (1 Cor. 8:6). And in saying this very thing, 'from whom, and through whom, and in whom are all things', we do not cut the nature apart, but confess the unity of nature, of will and of operation. So there is one God in these three, and these three are one God. That this is so the same Apostle confirms, saying: From him, and through him, and in him are all things: to him be glory for ages of ages, amen (Rom. 11:36). In agreement with this the prophet David says: May God, our God, bless us; may God bless us; and may all the ends of the earth fear him (Ps. 66:7-8). The Father, then, is Father without beginning; for there is nothing else from which the Father is: and the Son is Son, without beginning at least [in time]; for he is from the Father, and he is the creator of all times, and therefore does not take a beginning from time (John 1:1), because he is the Word, the power, the wisdom, which both made and precedes all time (1 Cor. 1:24). The Holy Spirit, however, is truly Spirit, proceeding indeed from the Father; but he is not himself also Son, because he is not begotten, but proceeds from the Father. For everything that is, is either unbegotten, or begotten, or made. There is, then, that which is neither born nor made; there is that which is born and is not made; and there is that which is neither born nor made; and there is that which is made and is not born; and there is that which is made and born and reborn; and there is that which is made and born and is not reborn. Now, mindful of what we have set out, let us assign the substances to each thing. That, then, which is neither born nor made is the Father: for he is not from anyone. That which is born and not made is the Son, who was begotten by the Father. That which is neither born nor made is the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father. That which is made and not born is heaven and earth and the other things that exist. That which is made and born and reborn is man, who is first born carnal and is reborn spiritual in baptism. That which is made and born and not reborn are the animals.

CHAPTER IV. To illustrate each of these, then, with examples: of the Father it is written thus: For there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things (1 Cor. 8:6); of the Son: One Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things (ibid.); and again: For there is one God, and one mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Tim. 2:5); of the Holy Spirit: For no one knows the things of a man, which are in him, except the spirit of the man which is in him: so also no one among men knows the things of God except the Spirit of God (1 Cor. 2:11); and again: But the Spirit searches even the depths of God (ibid. 10). That the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit are without beginning is shown from this: that what the Father is did not begin to be; and if he did not begin, neither did the Son begin; and the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father, did not begin either, because his procession is continuous, and is from him who did not begin: for the Father did not begin to be, and because he did not begin, neither did the Spirit begin to be; for the reason that he is both in him and of him. Of the Son again, that he did not begin, the evangelist testifies, saying: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. This was in the beginning with God (John 1:1-2). So because he was, he did not begin; and because he was with God, he did not begin; and because he was God, he did not begin; and because this one was in the beginning with God, he did not begin: for God was so born from God that he knows no beginning. Neither, then, is the Father cheated because he is unbegotten, or because he begot the Son; nor is the Son cheated because he was begotten, or because he is begotten from the unbegotten; nor is the Holy Spirit cheated because he is of both, that is, of the Father and the Son. Yet he is theirs in such a way that he is not poured back into either the Father or the Son; because he is God, having neither beginning nor any end, inasmuch as he is co-eternal with the Father and the Son; because he breathes where he will, and on whom he will, and on as many as he will, and as much as he will, by his own will (John 3:8). He fills, then, with his grace whom he will, and as many as he will, and as much as he will; he himself is not filled: he gives perfection, he does not receive it: he sanctifies, but is not himself sanctified.

CHAPTER V. — This one, then, like the Father and the Son, is both life and life-giving, both light and illuminating, both good and goodness, both holy and holiness (Rom. 8:15): this is the Spirit of adoption; this is he who divides his gifts to each as he will (1 Cor. 12:11): this is the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, of knowledge and piety, of counsel and strength, and of the fear of God (Isa. 11:2): this is the Holy Spirit, through whom the Father is acknowledged and the Son is glorified; by whom alone he himself is known, and who alone knows all that is theirs through unity of nature: this is he of whom the Son said: And my Father will give good things to those who ask him (Matt. 7:11), that is, either himself or all his graces. Just as, then, the Lord Christ is called Word, and power, and wisdom, and righteousness, and pearl, and light, and way, and resurrection, and the other things that are written of him; so too the Holy Spirit is named [Spirit] of wisdom, understanding, counsel, strength, knowledge, piety and fear, as has already been said. Not, however, because he differs according to the differences of the names, but because one and the same is the fount and source of all the virtues, who has always dwelt in the Lord Christ, as sharer in his nature. These are the seven eyes which in the prophet Zechariah are said to be in one stone (Zech. 3:9), that is, in the Lord Christ. The property of each, then, is unchangeable: but there is always one worship, one veneration, one sanctification of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. For it is not fitting [to say] either that the Son was ever lacking to the Father, or that the Holy Spirit was ever lacking to the Son, as the impious heretics falsely claim. Let us, then, guarding against these things, keep the good resolve which we have received from the holy Fathers. Let us adore the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, understanding the Father in the Son, and the Father and the Son in the Holy Spirit: distinguishing before we join, and joining before we distinguish: venerating the unity in the Trinity, and confessing the Trinity in the unity. The whole holy Trinity, then, is to be adored by us; because the whole is royal, because it is of one power and of one glory, above the world, above the ages, uncreated, invisible, incomprehensible, unsearchable: in what order it is within itself, it alone knows; but by us it is adored equally. In this invisible and ineffable holy Trinity we ought to understand nothing so proper, so fixed, as peace and quiet. For there is no dissension in the nature of God, since it must not be thought able to be dissolved, inasmuch as it is always peace and love. For if four substances, that is, heat, blood, phlegm and moisture, make a man, and he is one man, how do you not understand the Trinity in the unity, or the unity in the Trinity? God the Father almighty, then, having an almighty Word and Spirit, is above human understanding, and beyond what can be thought, incomprehensible and eternal: whom we can come to know, as far as the measure of our weakness permits, only when we have come to know the Lord Christ, who is his form and his only Son; because, as he himself says: He who has seen the Son has seen the Father also, who sent him, and who is in him, and who abides in him (John 14:9); and again: And this is eternal life, that they may know you the true God, and Jesus Christ, whom you have sent (John 17:3). The almighty Father, then, obtained the name of Father through the Son; because no one can be or be called a father without a son, nor a son without a father. And it is a thing of honour to confess the only-begotten Son of God, the Word and wisdom, and his Holy Spirit, as substantially equal in all things to the Father. For who has in truth fitted a colour, or a shape, or a size to the Word and wisdom, insofar as it is wisdom, or to the Holy Spirit, so as to seek degrees there and make ranks, where all things remain for ever invisible, united and at peace?

CHAPTER VI. — First of all, then, it must be believed that there is one God, who made all things from nothing through his Word, and gave them life through the Holy Spirit: who, while he contains all things, is himself contained by no one. That this is so the prophet David comprised in one short verse, saying: By the Word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power (Ps. 32:6). This is the Holy Spirit who in the beginning and at the fashioning of the world was borne over the waters (Gen. 1:2). This is he in whom Moses and Aaron performed signs before Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and of whom the magicians said: This is the finger of God (Exod. 8:19). This is he who spoke in Moses, and in all the holy patriarchs and prophets and apostles (2 Pet. 1:21); of whom the Apostle says: And we have all been given to drink of one Spirit (1 Cor. 12:13). This is he who fashioned the flesh of the Word of God in the sacred womb of the Virgin (Luke 1:35): this is he whom the Father sent upon the Son after the baptism (Matt. 3:16): this is he full of whose power Jesus returned from the Jordan and went back into Galilee (Luke 4:14): this is he whom the Father gives to those who ask him (Luke 11:13): this is he who is called by the Son our advocate with the Father, and another Paraclete, whom the Son promised that he would send to us (John 14:16). If, then, he were not of one nature with the Father and the Son, he would never be called by the Son another Paraclete: he is called another Paraclete for this reason, that we may recognise the equality of nature and power. The one, then, ascending from us to the Father, the other coming to us from the Father, declares the fatherly and most loving affection [shown] towards us always. He never allows us, in the temptations and miseries of this world, to be without an advocate or without a comforter. This is he who together with the Father sent the Son for the salvation of the human race, as the prophet Isaiah testifies, speaking in the person of the Son: The Lord has sent me, and his Spirit (Isa. 48:16; Matt. 12:28). This is he in whom Jesus cast out demons: this is he whom the Lord Jesus Christ, rising from the dead after the third day, gave to his disciples, saying: Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven; and whose you retain, they are retained (John 20:22–23). This is he who, descending upon the apostles on the day of Pentecost, imparted to them various tongues and graces (Acts 2:3), fulfilling the prophecy of the holy prophet Joel (Joel 2:28). This is he who, speaking in the holy martyrs, conquered the devil and the adversaries of Christ: this is he who filled Paul and set him apart for the apostleship (Acts 13:2). This is he who works his various gifts in the individual members of the Lord Christ until the end of the world (1 Cor. 12:6). This is he who not only drives from us sadness and grief and evil thoughts of base things, but also grants us remembrance of God within us, so that we may rightly say with the prophet David: I remembered God, and was delighted (Ps. 76:4); and again: I will be mindful of your wonders (ibid. 12). This is he who, coming to those of us who believe rightly and act well, [dispels] darkness and distress and faintness of heart, and, illuminating us with his light, mingles the mind of Christ with our mind; so that we may ponder our life, which is hidden in Christ, and consider what our state will be in the eternal ages to come, following Jesus the Son of God, who has passed through the heavens, and, sitting at the right hand of God and present in every place, has left nothing empty of his presence. Provided, however, that we do not think him to be contained in the space of one place on account of the dispensation of the body taken up for our salvation, nor think the nature of his divinity and incorporeality circumscribed. Divinity cannot be separated by difference of places; that this is so the Saviour himself proved, saying: No one has ascended into heaven except he who came down from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven (John 3:13). The Spirit, then, has no need of place to accomplish his works, [nor do] the Word, the power, the wisdom, the radiance, the image, the vapour, and the spotless splendour of God: all of which without doubt point to the person of the Son. There was, then, no time when the Father was without the Son, or the Son without the Father, or the Holy Spirit without the Father and the Son.

CHAPTER VII. — It is proper to God, then, not to have begun, but always to be the same, because he always is. That this is so God proves of himself, speaking to Moses: Go, and say to the children of Israel: He who is has sent me to you (Exod. 3:14). This is the Holy Spirit, who was neither born nor made, but is unmade, as are the Father and the Son. This is the Holy Spirit, who raises up the fallen and gives those who lie prostrate the opportunity to rise again, and dispenses each thing according to the variety of merits and the will of the Father and the Son, all of whose [things] he knows not by investigation but through unity of nature. He it is of whom the prophet says: The Spirit of the Lord is manifold, clean, undefiled and holy (Wisd. 7:22). As light, then, does not admit darkness, so the Holy Spirit also has it by nature that he is incapable of any filth. He it is who withdraws himself from thoughts that are without God. He it is who pours himself into holy souls and makes them friends of God and prophets. Unless, then, someone has had the Holy Spirit, neither the Father nor the Son, whose [Spirit] he is and with whom he is one God, come to him to make their dwelling with him. This is the spirit of wisdom, who is called manifold for this reason, that he has many things in himself; and what he has, that he also is, and he is one through all things, nor is he himself changed into any of the things which he works; like the image from a ring, which passes into the wax and does not leave the ring. That this is so the Lord proves, saying to Moses: I will take, therefore, of the Spirit which is in you, and give it to those seventy (Num. 11:17), as if, that is, fire were transferred from a small flame without loss to the one from which it is taken. On account of this unchangeableness and diverse working, then, it was said by the Lord of holy John the Baptist that he came in the spirit and power of Elijah (Luke 1:17). This is he whom God sent into our hearts crying: Abba, Father (Gal. 4:6); and in whom we cry: Abba, Father; for both are said, both that we have received the Spirit crying: Abba, Father, and that we have received the Spirit in whom we cry: Abba, Father (Rom. 8:15). He has explained, then, what he said, 'crying', that is, making us cry. This is the Spirit who intercedes for us with unutterable groanings, when human frailty does not know what it ought to pray for (ibid. 26). This the holy Apostle taught us in himself not only by word but also showed us by his own example (2 Cor. 12:7–8), when, not knowing [it was] against his own benefit and perfection, he prayed that the goad of the flesh which buffeted him might depart from him: [the goad] which afterwards, instructed by the Holy Spirit himself, he said had been given him for this reason, lest he be lifted up by the greatness of his revelations and suffer some loss of good. But because the Lord loved him, who has always been accustomed to show the power of his divinity through every weak thing, he did not do what he was asking in ignorance. He is the Holy Spirit who, in the catholic Church spread through the whole world, pours himself out as the fountain of all graces. This is the Spirit of the Lord Jesus (ibid. 9), who at the end of the world will slay the antichrist by his power (2 Thess. 2:8). This is the Holy Spirit whom none of the heretics has; who, although they all think they have him in the baptism of Christ, yet unless they come to the Church of Christ, will not be able to have the Spirit of Christ. That this is so the blessed apostle Paul proves, saying: If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his (Rom. 8:9). And again: No one can say, Lord Jesus, except in the Holy Spirit (1 Cor. 12:3). Confirming this, the blessed John, apostle and evangelist (1 John 4:2–3), says: By this the Spirit of God is known: every spirit which confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God, and every spirit which dissolves Jesus is not from God; and this is the antichrist, of whom you have heard that he is coming, and now he is already in the world; and again: Who is it that overcomes the world, but he who believes that Jesus is the Son of God (1 John 5:5 ff.)? This is he who came through water and blood, Jesus Christ, not in water only, but in water and blood. And it is the Spirit who testifies that Jesus is the truth; for there are three who bear witness on earth, the spirit, the water and the blood, and the three are one.

CHAPTER VIII. — Justly, then, will he say at the judgement to those who confess him as Lord without the Holy Spirit: Why do you call me Lord, Lord, and have not done what I said (Luke 6:46)? And, not gathering with me, you have scattered the peoples and my members, for whom I shed my blood? And therefore the offering of the heretics, who do not have the Holy Spirit, profits not for the worship of God but for the worship of demons. For whatever the heretics speak in their synagogues, that is, in the little assemblies of Satan, is not the teaching of the Lord, but the howling and the tricks of their demons. For these are the ones of whom the Holy Spirit, through the prophet Isaiah, says that the Jewish people gave themselves to a table, saying: You prepared a table for Fortune (Isa. 65:11); and therefore the Apostle rebukes both them and the sinners who, not judging themselves, boldly approach the sacrosanct body and blood of Christ, saying: You cannot partake of the table of the Lord and of the table of demons; you cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons (1 Cor. 10:21). Let these things said about the offering of the heretics suffice; now let us return to our order.

CHAPTER IX. — Whatever, then, we have said of the Holy Spirit, that this is likewise done both by the Father and by the Son we have left untouched and undiscussed, since we know for certain that the holy and inseparable Trinity never works anything outside itself. And so that what I have said may be clear, I will set it out briefly. The Trinity made the incarnation of the Word, and yet the incarnation belongs only to the Word (Augustine, Against the Sermon of the Arians 15). The Trinity made the voice from heaven over the Son after the baptism, and yet it belongs only to the Father. The Trinity made the coming of the Holy Spirit upon the Son in the form of a dove (Luke 3:22), and yet it belongs only to the Holy Spirit. This threefold working abiding in unity the blessed Apostle proves, saying: For there are divisions of graces, but one Spirit; and there are divisions of ministries, but one Lord; and there are divisions of workings, but one God who works all things in all (1 Cor. 12:4 ff.). These three, then, grant one grace to believers, because the substance of the holy and inseparable Trinity is not one and then another. When, therefore, the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit are each said to work, yet they work all things equally. He founded by Wisdom, gave life by the Spirit, and ordered by just judgement. He, then, by his justice distributed the world into various forms, and, his grace ordering it, incomprehensibly disposes, holds together and governs its members, so great as they are: and the government of his providence is so just, so secret, so hidden, that what is thought a punishment is medicine for the sufferer. One God, then, subsisting in the holy Trinity, works these things: proving which of himself, he says through the prophet Isaiah: I am the Lord, and there is no other besides me (Isa. 45:6–7), that is, apart from my Word and my Spirit, my power and my wisdom, which is always in me; there is no other God and saviour, of whom the same prophet says: And the Lord will send them a saviour, who will save them from their sins (ibid. 5). And again, in the person of the Father, the prophet written above says: By myself I have sworn, that a word shall go out of my mouth, and shall not return to me empty (Isa. 19:20; 45:23; 55:11). In truth the Word of the Father did not return to him empty, because he placed at the right hand of the Father the soul and the pledges of our salvation, that is, the true [soul] and the true body he had taken up. Seeing in the Spirit that this would be so, the prophet says: Truly you are a hidden God (Isa. 45:15), that is, in the flesh, the God of Israel, the Saviour; and again: His face hidden and despised (Isa. 53:3); that is, so that the divine power might be concealed by a human body; and again: And he is a man, and who knows him (Jer. 17:9)? And again: This is our God, no other shall be accounted beside him, who was seen on earth and lived among men (Baruch 3:36); and again: A man in sorrow, and knowing how to bear infirmities (ibid.); by these words showing, that is, the true body of a man and the true soul, who, knowing how to bear infirmities, overcame [them] by his divinity, making peace through the blood of his cross, whether the things in heaven or the things on earth (Isa. 53:4; Col. 1:20). For it has been made clear by these words that in the Lord Jesus Christ there is not truth in part and falsehood in part, but all truth is in him, that is, [the truth] both of God and of man.

CHAPTER X. — But human wisdom does not understand this, which the blessed Apostle condemns, saying: Let your faith not be in the wisdom of men, whose thoughts the Lord knows, that they are vain, but in the power of God (1 Cor. 2:5); and again: Not taught by the words of human wisdom, but taught by the Holy Spirit (ibid. 13). Therefore let faith not be in the wisdom of men, and there is no heresy. The Son and the Holy Spirit, then, are always in the Father; and that this is so the Son himself confirms, saying: I and the Father are one (John 10:30): one on account of the nature of the divinity, are on account of the properties of the persons; and again: Behold, the hour comes... that you will leave me alone; and I am not alone, because the Father is with me (John 16:32); and again: The works which I do, the Father, abiding in me, he himself does them (John 14:10). He, then, is the Son always in the Father, who says to Moses: He who is has sent me to you (Exod. 3:14). He it is in whom the Father rejoiced when the world was completed, because he had founded so great a mass of earth upon the seas and had set it upon the rivers, so that the heaviest element hung by his will upon the thin waters. In the establishing of the world, then, when the Father was making firm its foundations, no one was with him except those who were in him, that is, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Let the impious heretics therefore blush, who say that the Son of God or the Holy Spirit is a creature, or that there was a time when they were not; for the founder of times does not have a beginning at any time. Whatever, therefore, the Son speaks are the words of the Father and are the words of the Holy Spirit; whatever the Father speaks are the words of the Son, are the words of the Holy Spirit; whatever the Holy Spirit speaks are the words of the Father, are the words of the Son of God. Therefore by these words the knowledge of the One who fills all things, and in whom all things are, is proclaimed under the mystery of the Holy Trinity; for the Son says: The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father (John 15:26); yet on account of the fellowship and unity of nature he is sent by the Son; and the Son was seen by the prophet Isaiah in the guise of one reigning, but on account of the partnership of majesty and the unity of substance the Holy Spirit spoke in the prophet. In the Cherubim, indeed, and the Seraphim, where that vision is described as having taken place, the Lord is in part shown and in part concealed; for with two wings they veiled his face, and with two they veiled his feet, and with two they flew (Isa. 6:2). Veiled, therefore, are the things which were before the world, and the things which will be after the world, which neither eye has seen nor ear heard (1 Cor. 2:9); but the things which were made in six days have come to our knowledge through the sacred reading. We therefore confess in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit not only one operation but also equality; for where there is equality, there is the same nature and the same substance. For this reason, says the Evangelist (John 5:18), the Jews persecuted him, because he not only broke the sabbath, but also, by calling himself the Son of God, made himself equal to God. This the Lord himself confirms, saying: I and the Father are one, and I am in the Father, and the Father is in me; and again: What the Father has given me is greater than all; and no one can snatch [it] from my hand; and at once he adds: And no one can snatch [it] from the hand of the Father (John 10:30; 14:10; 10:29). If, then, no one can snatch from the hand of the Son what the Father has given, and these same things are in the hand of the Father, and are not snatched from him, it is clearly proved that all things of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, who is both of the Father and of the Son, are common; and that what is the Father's is held in the Son's hand, and what is the Son's is held in the Father's hand. The Lord Christ, therefore, son of God and of man, who was always with the Father and in the Father, spoke in two ways, that is, now according to the glory of his divinity, now according to the man of our nature that he had taken up. The Father, then, is in the Son, and the Son in the Father, and the Holy Spirit is in both; and therefore the right confession of the mystery of the holy and inseparable Trinity is our ignorance; for since the holy Apostle testifies that the judgements of God are inscrutable (Rom. 11:33), the wise reader understands how inscrutable and hidden he himself must be whose [judgements] are inscrutable and hidden. Yet the holy Apostle did not say: The judgements of God are found with difficulty, or never; lest he should seem to cut off entirely the hope of those who seek; but he says: The judgements of God are inscrutable. However much, then, someone may advance in knowledge and, devoted to wisdom, probe hidden things, yet created nature can never comprehend the substance of the uncreated. For when he has found some things, other things again present themselves for inquiry; when he has discovered those, he will find countless others as well. So much material is always supplied to the one who investigates that ignorance of the rest envelops the knowledge of the former. Hence the most wise Solomon too, knowing the natures of things and their difficulties, and setting a measure to his own wisdom, says: I said, I will become wise, and it withdrew further from me than it was, and its lofty depth, who will find it? And again: For many works of the Lord are hidden; and again: Just as you do not know what is the way of the spirit, and by what means the bones are fitted together in the womb of a pregnant woman, so you do not know the works of God, who is the maker of all things; and again: Do not seek things higher than you, and do not search out things stronger than you; and again: Just as it is not good for one who eats much honey, so he who is a searcher of majesty is overwhelmed by glory (Wisd. 7:17; Eccl. 7:24 and 25; 11:5; [Sir.] 3:22). And truly nothing is so true, nothing so evident; for it is written: Who understands sins (Ps. 18:13)? If, then, men do not understand their own sins, how much less will they be able to discover the nature of God and his counsels! Confirming this, the prophet says: Who has declared his generation (Isa. 53:8)?

CHAPTER XI. — In this one God, then, the Father almighty, we believe, the founder of things visible and invisible, whose judgements and counsels are hidden, but never unjust. This Father, however, is Father without any father of his own; and therefore the Son begotten of him, whose generation human speech cannot declare, cannot be inferior to him; for, as has been said, he is his Word, power and wisdom. We therefore acknowledge [him as] God and Lord, God the Son of God the Father most high, the only one of the only one, and we confess that with the Father and the Holy Spirit he is one God; and although human speech cannot unfold his equality, yet we have learned the sacrosanct and venerable mysteries of his incarnation from the holy Archangel Gabriel addressing the holy virgin Mary, who, made pregnant by the word, alone aware, was wedded through the ear. For he says: The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; and therefore the holy one who will be born of you will be called the Son of God (Luke 1:35). This generation, then, by which he was born of the virgin for our salvation, does not make him later than the Father either in time or in power; for the begetter is not temporal, so that the Son should be disadvantaged by time, since the eternal Father begot a coeternal Son; nor does the true faith hold him born or made from outside, as the heretics falsely say, but begotten from the very substance of the Father. It is honourable, therefore, to confess a true Son from the true God, in whom the eternity and omnipotence of the perfect and holy Trinity consist; and therefore, as it befits us to believe in the Father, so also in the Son; for he who was begotten is altogether that which he who begot is. We believe also in the Holy Spirit, whose majesty, power and equality, which he possesses with the Father and the Son, we have already shown above by his own gift: proceeding from the Father, and possessing deity, operation and substance in common with the Father and the Son; and distinguishing the persons in their properties, we nonetheless confess the deity of the holy Trinity to be inseparable; for what we divide by names and persons, this we join by power and deity and unity. The name of the holy Trinity, therefore, is a great mystery and secret; and therefore, when our discourse is about spiritual things, nothing at all of carnal things is to be set before the eyes of the heart. To the holy and inseparable Trinity, then, belong invisible light, inseparable power, incomprehensible substance, unending life, at whose side stands all everlasting peace, which no creature ever penetrates, none disturbs. If anyone, therefore, places either the Son or the Holy Spirit outside the majesty of the Father, he seems to seek hope for himself from himself, that is, from a like nature, not from a higher one; for everything that is created, as far as this is concerned, was made from what was not, and is like itself. To the Lord Christ, therefore, God is Father by [his] own generation, but to us by voluntary adoption; to him he is father by nature, to us by grace; to him he is God by unity of mystery, but to us by power. Whoever, then, holds otherwise than this, and does not so believe, let him be anathema.

CHAPTER XII. — The Holy Spirit, moreover, is he who, as has already been said, is of both the Father and the Son: he it is who, like the Father and the Son, fills the world; he it is who was declared holy and good by the Son; he it is who is declared good and right by the prophet David, just as the Lord Christ is (Luke 11:13); for he says: The Word of the Lord is right, this of the Son; and: My heart has poured forth a good Word. But of the Holy Spirit: Renew a right Spirit within me; and: Your good Spirit will lead me into the right way (Ps. 1:14; 32:4; 44:1; 50:12; 142:10). He it is who foresees future things as though present; he it is who foretold to us, very many years beforehand, the birth of the Lord Christ, his wonders, persecution, passion, cross, death, burial, resurrection, ascension into heaven, and his coming to judgement. Just as the Father, then, is without beginning, so he also has the Holy Spirit and the Son coeternal without beginning, begotten from himself, not after himself. And therefore, just as the Father precedes all antiquity of times, outlasts [it] by eternity, surpasses [it] by length of age, so too he begot the Son as his partner both in power and in this equality which we have spoken of; but this Power, this Wisdom, this Word, which is the Son, to use the words of the Apostle (Phil. 2:6 ff.), though he was in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal to God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of men, and found in appearance as a man. He humbled himself even to death, and the death of the cross, for which reason God also exalted him and gave him a name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of things in heaven, on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father. On account of this mystery, therefore, the Son of God is called Christ; which [name], however, signifies his birth according to the flesh, his passion and death: but this wonderful and singular birth, by which Christ was born, came about from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, as the faith of the holy creed testifies. This, then, who is the only Son of God in divinity, is found to be the only one also in the fleshly birth through which he took up our manhood in order to save it; for he alone was born of a Virgin, who felt neither conception from a man nor corruption from childbirth. We confess, therefore, that he was born according to the flesh of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary; for so, as has already been said, the Archangel Gabriel had promised to the blessed Virgin Mary that it would be, saying: The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; and therefore the holy thing that will be born of you will be called the Son of God (Luke 1:35). This Son of God was crucified under Pontius Pilate for our salvation, and buried. True flesh, therefore, was taken from the Virgin, true [flesh] was crucified, true [flesh] was buried, true [flesh] was raised again after the third day. To the womb of the holy Virgin, then, the Holy Spirit came as maker and sanctifier, both to take flesh from there and to form a man there; so that by the joining of the Word and the man from the first forming, Christ, the mediator of God and men, might be born perfect, arising without deceit as to his humanity, without corruption of his deity: about to die, because created; but about to overcome the bonds of death, as Creator. No separation, therefore, is to be asserted between the Word and the man taken up by him, because we confess one Christ, the Son of God, out of two natures, that is, divine and human, joined together in a mystical manner.

CHAPTER XIII. — It is permitted to us, therefore, to believe these things, not to dispute them: to seek humbly, not to inquire proudly. The Word, then, and substance of God, which is in all respects incorporeal, could not be inserted into a human body except through the mediation of some spiritual nature, that is, the soul. So, with the soul first receiving the Word of God in [its] rational secret place, God was born of a Virgin without any contact of a man. Just as, then, the Son of God, offering himself to all as an example by participation in himself, is not diminished by the communion of participation, inasmuch as he is the Word and Wisdom of God; so the holy soul of Jesus, which for our sins was both sorrowful and troubled, contracted nothing from that. This is she whom God loved above his fellows (Ambrose, On Luke, bk. 10, 127): this is our life, of which the Apostle says: And your life is hidden with Christ in God (Col. 3:3): this is she who loved justice and hated iniquity (Ps. 44:8): this was sorrowful not for death, but even to death (Matt. 26:38): this was troubled on the cross not for herself but for us: not the Power, not the Wisdom, not the Word of God, who took her up for the salvation of our souls, and, adorning her with every beauty of virtues and holiness, brought her into fellowship with the deity. Of this [soul], then, which is in all respects like our souls, the Saviour says: I have power to lay down my soul, and to take it up again; and: No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of myself, and take it up again (John 10:18). This is the blessed soul which on the cross cried out to the divinity, saying: God, my God, look upon me, why have you forsaken me (Matt. 27:46)? The man, therefore, cried out, being about to die by separation from the divinity: for since the divinity is free of death, death certainly could not occur unless life departed, because the divinity is life; for what is always immortal and incorrupt never suffers either death or corruption. God, therefore, who is Word and Spirit, who breathes where he wills (John 3:8), did not abandon the flesh or soul he had taken up against his will: but because he willed, where he willed, how he willed, and when he willed, leaving it, he laid it down, and took it up again. He was not, therefore, stripped of the flesh by anyone's right and power, but he stripped himself; for he who is able not to die, if he did not wish to, without doubt died because he willed it. Confirming that this is so, the Apostle says: Stripping himself of the flesh, he despoiled the principalities and powers, triumphing over them in himself (Col. 2:15), namely through the death of the man taken up; so that, as the same blessed Apostle says, through the death of the man taken up he might destroy him who had the dominion of death (Heb. 2:14), that is, the devil, and might free those who through their whole life were subject to slavery. That this would be so the prophet Isaiah had foretold long before, saying: As a sheep is led to the slaughter, and as a lamb before its shearer, he was dumb; and again: He was offered because he himself willed it, to take away the sins of many; and again: He delivered his soul to death, and was reckoned with the wicked; and he bore the sins of many, and he prayed for the transgressors (Isa. 53:7 ff.). Not, therefore, by necessity, but by will did the Lord Christ endure the cross, saying to Peter, who through the frailty of fear was scandalised at the mystery of the cross and trembled with human dread: Get behind me, Satan, you are a stumbling block to me; for you do not savour the things that are of God, but those that are of men. For the cup which the Father has given me, you do not want me to drink it (Matt. 16:23; John 18:11; Matt. 26:23). Otherwise, if he had not been offered by his own will and had not willed to endure the cross, could he who was able to point out and foretell the betrayer, and was saying to the apostles: All of you will take offence at me this night (Matt. 26:31), not have been able to evade those who had been sent to arrest him? He went to meet them fearlessly and said: Whom are you seeking (John 18:4)? And at once they fell backwards, because they could not bear the voice of God present. It was not, therefore, a matter of necessity that he suffered, but of will; and not so much his own, but also the Father's, to whom he says: I willed to do your will, my God (Ps. 39:9). Through the true flesh, then, of the immortal mediator of God and men, we mortals have been redeemed, given life, saved and freed from the snares and captivity of the devil, over whom he gave us power, saying: Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the might of the enemy (Luke 10:19). The whole incarnation of humility and mystery, therefore, took place for this, that we might receive power over the devil, who, though knowing himself to be a thing made, through pride fell into such madness that he wished to make himself equal to the most high Creator, saying: I will set my throne in the north, and I will be like the Most High (Isa. 14:13). That this is so the Apostle confirms, saying: For what was impossible for the Law, in that it was weak through the flesh, God, sending his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and of sin, that is, of the first man, condemned sin in the flesh; so that, as in Adam all die, so also in Christ, who through the passion of the cross dedicated to us from his side a washing and a drink by martyrdom, all might be made alive (Rom. 8:3; Col. 2:15; 1 Cor. 15:22).

CHAPTER XIV. For this reason, then, it is fitting for us to consider more carefully who offers, to whom he offers, what he offers, and for whom he offers, he who has become for us the way, the truth and the gate; of which gate the Holy Spirit says through the Prophet: This is the gate of the Lord, the just shall enter by it (Ps. 117:20); and again: He shall not be put to shame when he speaks with his enemies in the gate (Ps. 126:5). But to that gate none will come except those who have deserved, through the grace and help of God, to be lifted up from the gates of death, that is, from sins. So I recall with steadfast profession the sufferings of him in whom I believe, and I am not ashamed of what the Redeemer of the world both underwent for my salvation and overcame by his own power. You may laugh, Jew and Gentile, that I place my hope in one whom I profess to have been crucified and to have died; yet I glory in these wounds, through which I understand, what you do not know, that I am pleasing to my Redeemer: for the word of the cross, as the Apostle says, is folly to those who are perishing, but to those who are to be saved it is the power of God (1 Cor. 1:18). See, I make mention of Pilate the judge, by whom he was judged who is to be the judge of the world. Why should the sufferings of that blessed body, which a swift resurrection followed and undid, gnaw at the dignity of my faith? For this is not the end of my faith and confession: but hear what follows. On the third day he rose again from the dead, ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of the Father, and from there he will come to judge the living and the dead (Acts 10:42), that is, both the just and sinners, both Gentiles and Jews, both souls and bodies. Does our belief not now seem to you firm and happy, which rests on him whom not even death itself could withstand and resist?

CHAPTER XV. Indeed, never did it appear more clearly how abundant were the mercy and patience of our Redeemer than when he undertook the office of this mystery, that is, that by taking up our substance he should also take up the laws of the gibbet and the tomb. His adversities, therefore, were spent for our prosperity, and in our Redeemer the divine and human natures entered into a kind of sacred exchange with one another; so that divinity received testimony from humanity, and humanity received a reward from divinity, that is, so that by the wounds of his body our God might show the greatness of his love toward us, and so that both our soul and our body might recognise that the grace of obedience is repaid to them by fellowship with the divinity. We must consider, then, with what faith and with what devotion we ought to cleave to and serve this Lord, so bountiful in such great gifts toward us, who set no limit to his giving, so that he gave to the faithful as a reward as much as he himself possessed in his kingdom: so that we might even believe that we can become his co-heirs, he revealed himself as a sharer even of our nature; not, however, to thrust [his] substance down from the citadel of divinity, but to draw us, weak and living in the utmost baseness and necessity of death, to the glory of the resurrection. For he showed in himself whatever he promised us; and by rising again he taught that the substance of this flesh does not perish: and by his ascension he showed where its dwelling would be after the resurrection. This, then, is the great, truly great sacrament of godliness, which the Teacher of the Gentiles announced to have been manifested in the flesh (1 Tim. 3:16), as the outcome of events also [showed]. And it is clear that it was justified in the Spirit; since the mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Tim. 2:5), gave us an example not only of the happiness to be hoped for, but also of the truth to be laid hold of. This sacrament of godliness, through which our Maker and Redeemer embraces us, as it shone with the testimony of power, so also, taken up in glory at the ascension, it was celebrated by the services of the Angels; and therefore the nature of human flesh is not to be despised, which deserved through the Lord Christ to enter into the substance and fellowship of the holy Trinity. I think indeed that, by God's gift, enough has been said about the mystery of the holy Trinity and the incarnation of the Lord Saviour: but since the resurrection of our flesh is placed at the end of our doctrine, the same things must be repeated by us more firmly and more often because of the heretics.

CHAPTER XVI. For the Word of God, who is the Lord Christ, who is the firstborn of every creature and the firstborn from the dead, came to his own image, which he himself had formerly made; of which image it is written: And God formed man after his own image and likeness (Gen. 1:27); and taking up flesh for the sake of flesh, with the rational soul as mediator, from the holy virgin Mary, and purifying like things by like, that is, soul and flesh, he became man in all things without sin. With the soul, then, mediating between God and the flesh, he who, as the Apostle says, makes all rich became poor, so that by his poverty we might be enriched with divine and heavenly riches (2 Cor. 8:9): through that sign of salvation which God gave to the human race, as the prophet Isaiah says (Isa. 7:14 ff.): Behold, the Lord will give you a sign, behold, a Virgin will conceive in the womb and bear a son, and his name will be called Emmanuel, which is interpreted, God with us: who, before he knew how to call his father or his mother, ate butter and honey, that is, he was filled with the Holy Spirit, whose teaching is sweeter to us than honey and the honeycomb: who, receiving the spoils of Samaria from the Magi, was proved man, king and God. Of this wonderful sign also holy Simeon says to the virgin Mary: Behold, this one is set for the fall and for the rising of many in Israel, and for a sign that will be spoken against (Luke 2:34). Of which sign the blessed apostle Paul also says: The Jews ask for signs, and the Greeks seek wisdom (1 Cor. 1:22). For the sake of his image, then, which he had made in the first man, and which he had seen disfigured in man by the craft of the devil, Christ came in the likeness of sin, so that through the passion of the cross and death he might call man back to his former image (Rom. 8:3): an image which can indeed be darkened through neglect, but cannot be destroyed by nature. Of this image the Prophet says: Although man walks in the image of God, yet he is disquieted in vain (Ps. 38:7). There is no one, then, who does not bear some image, that is, either of holiness or of sin. We walk in the image of God when the good thoughts which have been implanted in us by God remain in us and lead us to good works. The remembrance of God, then, shuts out from our heart all the crimes and sins which the devil strives to sow and paint in our heart. Hence it is said by the Prophet: Lord, in your city you will bring their images to nothing (Ps. 72:20). It profits nothing, then, to have read or heard, unless you have laid up the good things you have read or heard in the treasury of memory. As, then, there are three things in man, that is, body, soul and spirit, so there are three more prominent things which lead us either to good or to evil, that is, thought, speech or action. These three the Holy Spirit briefly comprehends in the first psalm, saying: Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, and has not stood in the way of sinners, and has not sat in the chair of pestilence (Ps. 1:1). These are the three grooms of the devil, who lie in wait for the wretched soul, so as to rouse it to sin either in word, or in deed, or in thought. With spirit, soul and body, then, we do either well or ill; we are either chaste or we commit fornication: and therefore, as the greedy and robbers are slaves of mammon, and as gluttons and drunkards are slaves of the belly and of lust, so every sin lords it over men, as the prophet proves, saying: There shall be five cities in the land of Egypt, speaking the language of Canaan (Isa. 19:18), that is, the five fleshly senses, which speak to the wretched soul oppressed by the darkness of Egypt; for Egypt is interpreted as persecuting, or afflicting and constraining. Unless, then, we overcome the north wind, the coldest wind, by the warmth of faith, with the help of Christ, who [...] good things and delights [...], at once it will stir up in us the heat of desire and lust. Let the flesh, then, be worn down by fasting, and circumcised with the knife against every desire, and let sin not reign in our mortal body (Rom. 6:12), so that we may escape the fellowships of the world and the reproaches of the devil. Fasting, then, is the contrition and humbling of the soul, and the affliction of the body.

CHAPTER XVII. — Let what has been said about the image of God, to which man was made, suffice. Now let us return to the order [of the creed]. He was born, then, of a virgin mother among men, without a human father; for he had God as Father in heaven, whom he had not come to deny by being born of another. Because of the sentence on the virgin Eve (Gen. 3:16), which she received after the sin, who, though she was immortal, was made mortal after the transgression, he himself came through a Virgin: and as death gained dominion through a virgin, so through the virgin Mary came he who was to conquer death. The occasion of death entered through a tree, but by the death of the Lord it was shut out through a tree: the woman was brought forth from the side of the sleeping man (Gen. 2:23); and likewise the Church was formed from the side of Christ on the cross, through the passion and the sleep of death. The woman was formed from the side of the man; and therefore the Lord is struck in the side, so that the man might suffer for the woman, she who was formed from his side and who persuaded him. But let us now see, since the place requires it, what answer must be given to the heretics who will have it that the soul of Adam is either a portion of God, or was made before his body was fashioned from the earth: which is wholly foreign and alien to the catholic faith. For it is written that God fashioned man from the clay of the earth, and after the fashioning breathed into him the breath of life; and man became a living soul (Gen. 2:7; cf. ch. 15, 11). That this is so the example of the woman Eve teaches us, who, when she had been formed into a woman from the rib of Adam, afterwards received a soul from God; and this form of creation is kept in us until the end of the world, as the prophet Isaiah testifies, saying: Who forms the spirit of man in him; and David: Who fashioned their hearts one by one (Ps. 32:15). So, according to so evident an example, the soul is neither prior to the body, nor created beforehand, nor from the substance of God, nor did it, as the heretics will have it, live long before, somewhere or other, in bodily and irrational creatures: and they have nothing by which to prove this.

CHAPTER XVIII. — Daily, then, the God of majesty makes souls in bodies already fashioned, and sends them in, as Moses the lawgiver testifies concerning pregnant women who carry an infant formed or not yet formed (Exod. 21:22–23). That this is so the Lord confirms, saying: My Father works until now, and I work (John 5:17). As, then, it is impious to say that the soul of man is from the substance of God, or that soul comes from soul, so it is impious to say that it was made before the fashioning of the body; since Adam himself proclaims, saying: This now is bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh (Gen. 2:23). God, then, is one thing, the soul of man another; for it was made by him, not from him. For God is invisible, incorruptible, impenetrable, undefilable, who can be corrupted in no part, and who can be harmed in no part: but the soul of man, which is not God, is capable of sin, and lives in hardship, and is led into falsehood, is saddened, is blinded, is troubled, is corrupted, is taken captive; and therefore it needs the power of a deliverer. This change of the soul, then, this variability, shows me plainly that the soul of man is neither God nor of his substance; for if the soul of man is the substance of God, according to those who say this, then the substance of God is saddened, the substance of God is deceived, the substance of God is blinded, the substance of God is corrupted, the substance of God is taken captive; and now it is judged, and on the day of judgement, having taken up flesh, it will be condemned with the devil in eternal fire: how impious this is, anyone of sound mind understands. The Lord himself cries out, strengthening his apostles, and says: Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; but fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna (Matt. 10:28). Will God, then, according to these madmen, as has been said, judge a portion or nature of his own? Far from it. And therefore into those very bodies in which we were born, and from which our souls went out when we died, into those same [bodies] our souls enter after the resurrection at God's command; and they rise, if they have done good, to the resurrection of life, to receive the glory of the kingdom of heaven; but if they have done evil, to the resurrection of judgement and everlasting reproach and confusion. That it will be so the blessed Apostle confirms, saying: We must all be made manifest before the judgement seat of Christ, so that each may receive what belongs to his body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil (2 Cor. 5:10). For then, according to the prophecy of the prophet Isaiah (Isa. 24:2), there will be no difference between noble and base, priest and layman, slave and master, maidservant and her mistress, rich and poor, lender and him who is weighed down by debt, between buyer and seller (so Jerome on the same place of Isaiah). All, then, will stand equally before the judgement seat of Christ, and there will be no respect of persons with God. This holy Job also announces in almost the same words, saying: The small and the great are there, and the slave free from his master (Job 3:19). And the Saviour in the Gospel, to whom all judgement has been handed over because of the glorious passion of the man taken up, testifies in full words, saying: For when the Son of Man comes with the holy angels in the majesty of his Father, then he will repay each according to his works (Matt. 16:27; 25:31). All these things, then, will come to pass; for what is to come the Lord has spoken through the prophets, he who says: I have multiplied visions, and by the hand of the prophets I have been represented (Hos. 12:10).

CHAPTER XIX. — At this secret of the incarnation the prophet written of above marvels, and says: Watchman, what of the night? What of the night, watchman? My secret is mine, my secret is mine. Woe is me. When, says the prophet, I had heard these things (Isa. 21:11; 24:16), namely that the God of majesty was to put on flesh, and foresaw that the prophecy was to be fulfilled in him, I spoke to myself with the inward feeling of my heart; for I cannot tell all that I see: my tongue sticks to my throat, my voice is shut in by grief and fear, because such great mysteries are turning before my eyes. For I see as present the things that are to come: I understand that the watchman is that Samaritan of the man who, going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, fell among robbers (Luke 10:30). He is the watchman to whom blessed Job said (Job 7:20): O watchman of men, why have you set me against you, and I have become a burden to myself? Why do you not take away my sin, and why do you not remove my iniquity? He is the watchman who says: I am continually upon my watch, standing so many days and nights (Isa. 21:8); and of whom the Prophet says: Behold, he who keeps Israel will not slumber nor sleep (Ps. 120:4). Because of these terms, then, and because the persons in them very often change, and [because of] the parables, the prophets are obscure. But now let us return to the order.

CHAPTER XX. — The heretics who deny the resurrection of the flesh are accustomed, then, to set against us that testimony of the blessed Apostle in which he says: Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God (1 Cor. 15:50); cunningly keeping silent about what follows. For when he had said: Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God, he goes on and says: Nor will corruption possess incorruption (ibid.). These things, then, were said not so that the nature of our holy bodies should perish, but so that this corruptible should put on incorruption, as the same Apostle confirms, saying: So also is the resurrection of the dead; it is sown in corruption, it will rise in incorruption: it is sown in dishonour, it will rise in glory: it is sown in weakness, it will rise in power: it is sown an animal body, it will rise a spiritual body (ibid. 42 ff.). For these are the four orders of the resurrection, which were prefigured in that priestly rod which blossomed in the tabernacle of the Lord (Num. 17:8; Lev. 26:19). So, then, Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God is to be understood in the same way as what God threatens to the sinful people, saying: I will make the heaven that is above you bronze, and the earth that you tread iron: not that the nature of the elements is changed, but that by bronze and iron the greatness of the punishments is shown. The Lord Christ, then, showed us in himself that there will be a true resurrection, who after his resurrection on the third day showed the marks of the nails and the wound of the lance to his doubting disciples (Luke 24:40).

CHAPTER XXI. — Let us not, then, despise our flesh by living wickedly and luxuriously, the flesh in which the Lord Christ was both born and suffered, and rose again: let us not look down on the clay of our flesh, which, fired in the deity of the Lord Christ, which is fire, into the purest earthenware, reigns in heaven. It must certainly be asked why the Apostle said: For our God is a consuming fire (Heb. 12:29). For our God, who is living, divine and eternal fire, does not consume these bodily materials, but the consciences of sinners, and kindles our hearts in love of him. And for this reason the Angels, who are full of love, are themselves also called fire (Ps. 103:4). And so too are all the saints who have been kindled by that fire of which the Lord says: I came to send fire on the earth, and how I wish that it be kindled! (Luke 12:49); and again: Let your loins be girded, and burning lamps in your hands (ibid. 35). Of this the Apostle too said: Fervent in spirit, serving the Lord (Rom. 12:11). So the divine word is fiery and fervent. This the Lord himself confirms, saying to the prophet Jeremiah: Behold, I have given my words in your mouth like fire (Jer. 5:14); and the prophet himself declares that this fire was blazing within him, saying: And it became in my heart like a blazing fire (ibid. 20:9). So what was said, Our God is a consuming fire, was said not because God, who is spirit, is fire, but because he enlightens the just, while to those who undergo punishment he seems to be fire. So much about what was said: Our God is a consuming fire. Now let us return to the order.

CHAPTER XXII. — How, then, is the resurrection of the flesh denied, when long before, through the prophet, the Lord Christ said in his own person: My flesh rests in hope (Ps. 15:9); and in another place: His flesh will not see corruption (Acts 2:31); and again: His burial has been taken away; and again: And all flesh will see the salvation of God; and again: All flesh will come which is to worship in the sight of the Lord (Isa. 66:23; 1 Tim. 2:8), that is, either in the heavenly Jerusalem, or in every place where it fell or was buried, according to that saying of the Apostle: I want men to pray in every place, lifting up clean hands. For if the sun, which is a creature, and which is commanded to rise, is seen in the whole world and stretches out its rays, how much more must the Creator and almighty God be believed to be present in every place! To him the Prophet says: Where shall I go from your face? If I go down into hell, you are there (Ps. 138:7-8), and the rest. If, then, all flesh is to worship the Lord, and on the contrary the corpses of the men who have transgressed against God will be handed over to eternal burnings, on both sides there will be a true resurrection of the flesh. And therefore we must turn aside neither to the right nor to the left from this holy and catholic faith, that is, we must follow neither the Jewish nor the heretical error; of whom some, who are carnal, love only the flesh, while others, ungrateful for the benefits of God, refuse to have what the Lord Jesus Christ both had when born and possesses for ever in rising again. For this is the true resurrection, which so bestows glory on the flesh that it does not take away its reality, as has already been said; the Apostle says: This corruptible will put on incorruption, and this mortal will put on immortality; and again: We do not wish, then, to be stripped, understand of the flesh, but desiring to be clothed over with the glory which is from heaven; and again: That we may be found clothed and not naked, that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life (1 Cor. 15:53; 2 Cor. 5:2-4). No one, then, is clothed over unless he was first clothed; just as our Lord too, who was transfigured into glory on the mountain, at the time when he brought forward Moses and Elijah as witness to himself (Matt. 17:3); not only his garments but also his face shone like the sun; and where the face is named, I judge that the other members too were seen.

CHAPTER XXIII. — Into this glorification, then, all the just will be transformed in the resurrection, as John the Evangelist proves, saying: Beloved, we are sons of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him (1 John 3:2). And the just man says: But I shall appear in your sight with justice; I shall be satisfied when your glory is shown to me (Ps. 16:15). Our bodies, then, will rise to remain for ever, either for glory or for punishment (Dan. 12:2). Of this Elijah and Enoch are witnesses, who through so many series of years remain thus until the second coming of the Lord Christ. That this is so blessed Job confirms, saying: I know that my Redeemer lives, and on the last day I shall rise from the earth; and I shall again be surrounded by my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God. This my hope is laid up in my bosom (Job 19:25 ff.). Let the heretics, then, blush, who falsely claim either that the Lord's body was airy or phantasmal, or that ours will be, or [who claim] metempsychosis.

CHAPTER XXIV. — It is truly very impious and unjust that Job, who saw his wounds with his own eyes, and felt the rottenness and worms of his body with his own hands (Job 7:5), should be said to rise in another flesh or soul. What, then, we have said of blessed Job, [we say] of Peter, of Paul, and of all the saints who laid down their lives for God in various torments. The heretics indeed ask us mockingly whether in the resurrection there is a difference of sex, that is, whether women rise with men, blind men, not knowing the sentence of the Lord, who says: The queen of the south will rise in the judgement with the men of this generation, and will condemn them (Luke 11:31). Where, then, there is true flesh, there is difference of sex; and where there is difference of sex, there John is John, and Mary is Mary. The true resurrection of the flesh, then, will be without the works of the flesh; for as the Truth says: They will neither marry nor take wives, but they will be like the Angels in heaven (Matt. 22:30). A likeness to the angels, then, is promised us, the substance of the flesh is not denied; for when it is said, They will neither marry nor be given in marriage, it is said of those who can marry and yet will not marry. For if here, in this life, which is a trial upon earth, many, making themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven, do not marry; and not only men but women too do this with Christ's help: how much more in that blessed life, I will not say that this happens, but it will not even be permitted to think [otherwise]! It is, then, catholic and right to confess both sexes in the resurrection of the flesh, without the works of sex: since, as has already been said, while still placed in this life we strive with God's help not to fulfil the works of the flesh, which lusts against the spirit; as the Apostle proves, saying: You are not in the flesh but in the spirit (Rom. 8:9); for by denying that they were in the flesh, who clearly were in the flesh, he condemned in them not the substance of the flesh but the sins, that is, the works of the flesh; and again: That what is mortal may be swallowed up by life (2 Cor. 5:4); because though our outer man is corrupted, yet the inner is renewed: which we know happens not only in the kingdom of heaven and in baptism, but also daily in penitents, in whom the destruction of the flesh turns to spiritual progress. Then, therefore, there will be neither works of the flesh nor growth of members, nor will hair or nail grow: for we shall all rise into the perfect man, who is Christ (Eph. 4:13). For if for the Fathers in the desert for forty years neither hair nor nails grew, nor were garments or shoes worn out (Deut. 29:5), how impious it is to ask this concerning the kingdom of heaven, where pain and groaning and sorrow will flee away, the wise reader understands.

CHAPTER XXV. — But against this doctrine so true, so firm, and against proofs so clear and supported with all strength, the heretics are accustomed to set against us that saying of the Apostle (Tertullian, On the Resurrection, ch. 52): Not all flesh is the same flesh, but there is one flesh of man, another of cattle, another of birds (1 Cor. 15:39), and the rest; not understanding, wretched men, that the blessed Apostle spoke of difference in the honour of the body, not in its kind. There is one flesh of man, then, that is, of the servant of God, another of cattle, that is, of the heathen, and the sinner, and the heretic, who, when he was in honour, redeemed and honoured by the blood of Christ, did not understand, but was compared to senseless beasts and became like them (Ps. 48:13). Another of birds, that is, of the martyrs, who are borne up on the wings of the Holy Spirit and ascend to heavenly things.
