Another of fishes, that is, of those who are taken up after the water of the Saviour's baptism. One is the glory of the sun, that is, of Christ: another the glory of the moon, that is, of the Church: and another the glory of the stars, that is, of the seed of Abraham, and of those who show themselves his sons by faith and good works; for star differs from star in glory (1 Cor. 15:41), that is, those apostles and prophets who desired to see and hear Christ, and these who saw and heard him; and heavenly bodies and earthly bodies, that is, of Christians and of Jews. Finally, to show the resurrection of all, he concluded his statement thus, saying: So also is the resurrection of the dead (ibid. 42). That this may be so understood, let us set out examples from our condition as it is in this world. For when an infant has grown into a boy, and the boy into a youth, and the youth into a man, and the man into an old man, he in no way perishes through each age, but is always the same as he was. Little by little, then, here age perishes, but not nature. But in that heavenly Jerusalem, where this sun and moon will shine sevenfold, there will be no differences of ages; for there will be neither infant nor old man nor child who does not fill up his days, as being a son of the resurrection, and does not reach the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ, so that the span of years will neither fall short for anyone nor be in excess. In that time, then, when the age of all will be one, both saint and sinner will be made complete by a like resurrection, and will not differ among themselves in time: but one is drawn to eternal rewards and to receive good things a hundredfold, the other to eternal punishments. Though, then, in the human race men are born in one way and another, in the resurrection of the flesh the resurrection will be one and alike for all; for Adam was born in one way, Eve in another, Cain and Abel in another, and all men have been and are born in another; but in another way was born the man Christ Jesus, who is the mediator of God and men (Gen. 2:22; 4:1; 1 Tim. 2:5). Though, then, man is born from different beginnings, yet the one nature of man does not differ in the resurrection of the flesh and of all the members: all of which members are declared by one sentence of the Lord, when he spoke of that man who did not have a wedding garment (Matt. 22:11), nor kept that command: At all times let your garments be clean; whom he ordered to be bound hand and foot and taken away, so that he should not recline at the banquet, nor sit on the throne, nor stand at the right hand of God, but be sent into the Gehenna of fire, where there is weeping of eyes and gnashing of teeth (cf. Tertullian, On the Resurrection of the Flesh, ch. 35).

CHAPTER XXVI. — Further, it is quite impious to have doubts about our hairs, which the Lord indicated are numbered (Matt. 10:30). They were numbered in vain, then, if they are at some time to perish; but they do not perish, because we shall rise in the likeness of the Lord Christ with all our members. For if in this temporal fire, which consumes everything it takes in, almighty God showed his power in the three youths, whose hair he kept untouched in the furnace of burning fire (Dan. 3:50), will he not raise our hair in the resurrection? He will plainly raise it, without any increase or loss. There will be, then, no variation or difference in the resurrection of the dead, such as there is now the frail weakness of the flesh in us, which is pressed down by the mass of its own burden, which is painted, defiled, blinded, injured, wounded, healed, dies, is corrupted, and is returned to earth and dust; and yet after all these things, on the day of judgement, we shall be re-formed in the simple glory of the first and the second Adam. There will be, then, a true resurrection of the dead in the flesh, and a difference of sex, without the work of flesh and blood: The hour will come, says the Lord, in which all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God, and will come forth (John 5:28-29). They will hear, then, with ears, and come forth on feet, like Lazarus and all whom the Saviour raised (John 11:44). Those, then, will come forth from the tombs who had been carried into the tombs. All flesh, then, will come, not only from the earth, but also from the sea and from the rivers, to see the salvation of God (Tertullian, On the Resurrection of the Flesh, ch. 31). For he will command the fishes and the rivers of the sea, and the beasts of the earth and the birds of the sky, and they will belch up the bones and flesh of all the dead, so that they may rise, some to eternal life, others to reproach and everlasting confusion. Then the just will see the punishments and torments of the impious; for their worm will not die, and their fire will not be quenched, and they will be a sight to all flesh (Isa. 66:24). Since, then, we most truly hold this hope, just as we presented our members to serve uncleanness and iniquity unto iniquity (Rom. 6:19), so let us present them to serve justice unto sanctification of life, so that, rising from the dead, we may walk in newness of life, so that the life of the name of Jesus may be manifested in our mortal flesh because of his Spirit dwelling in us (2 Cor. 4:11; Rom. 8:11). It is just, then, and truly just, that we who have always carried about the dying of Christ in our body (2 Cor. 4:10), should have his life also manifested in our body. Stripping off, then, as the Apostle says (Col. 3:9), the old man with his deeds, let us not seek again the tunic of error and of sin, so that we may put on the new one, which is Christ (Eph. 4:24), imitating his bride, who says by night: I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I soil them (Song 5:3)?

CHAPTER XXVII. — This art of majesty and power, then, that is, the resurrection, is performed by that potter who speaks through the prophet Jeremiah to the sinful people, saying: Shall I not be able, like this potter, to re-form and restore you, house of Israel (Jer. 18:6)? He also showed this wonderful work of his majesty in the hand of Moses (Exod. 4:6-7), which, after it was changed to whiteness, he afterwards restored to its former colour. Moreover, the very word resurrection plainly signifies that it is not one thing that dies and another that is raised. What, then, dies in man, this is also brought to life. So, then, concerning the resurrection of the dead, whoever does not know [this], errs. Lastly, that wounded man of Jericho (Luke 10:34) is carried whole to the inn, and the wounds of his sins are healed with immortality through the grace of the merciful one. The prophecy, then, which was pending, has truly been fulfilled in the flesh of the Lord Christ, the prophecy which the Holy Spirit spoke, desiring to teach us; for he says: Who is this who comes up made white, leaning on her kinsman, and overflowing with delights? And again: My kinsman is white and ruddy (Song 8:5; 5:10). Ruddy, then, from the incarnation, but white from the divinity. That this is so blessed John the Evangelist confirms, when he says that the horse on which the Lord sat was red (Rev. 6:4), namely the holy body which he took from the holy Virgin. To him, as he ascends into heaven, it is said: Who is this who comes from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah? and: Why is your clothing red, and your garments like those of men treading in the winepress (Isa. 63:1-2)? And the sense is: Who is this who ascends from the earth, whose garments are sprinkled with blood? But as for what is said in the prophet Zechariah (Zech. 1:8), that horses of various colours followed him, that is, those who are shown either red in martyrdom, or starling-coloured in flight, that is, varied in virtues, or white in virginity. And that this red horse is described again as white by holy John (Rev. 19:11), shows his divinity, immortality and incorruption. And therefore all who follow him use not only white garments, [...] namely also immortal bodies. And therefore all the saints, with his help, imitate him; for they do not defile their garments, and by the gift of his grace they remain virgins. And therefore, as has been said, they will be in white garments, following the Lamb who took away the sin of the world.

CHAPTER XXVIII. — The whole man, then, as has been said, the Son of God took up from the Virgin, [and] he will raise him whole and entire, that is, soul and body, fulfilling his own saying, in which he says: All that the Father has given me, I shall not lose any of it; but I shall raise it up on the last day (John 6:39): a saying which we understand the Lord Christ to have spoken as much of himself as of his members, who speaks with his own mouth and that of his members in all the holy books. Both the head in the body, then, and the body in the head cry out to God, that is, both the Church in Christ and Christ in the Church; for in nothing are the members separated from the head, nor the head from the members. Then, therefore, his adversaries will see him, who pierced him and cried out: Away with him, away with him, crucify him (John 19:15). Then the prophecy of the Angels will be confirmed, who said to the astonished apostles: Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? He will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven (Acts 1:11). And certainly this must be asked, whether after the resurrection we are to eat (Tertullian, On the Resurrection of the Flesh, ch. 60) and drink in the kingdom of heaven, just as the Lord too after the resurrection ate and drank, to show a true body, and as Lazarus did (John 11:44), and the others whom he raised. The Lord ate, then, to show the reality of his body (Luke 24:43), and to strengthen the doubting apostles, who thought him a spirit and a phantom: he ate a honeycomb, to fulfil the prophecy which speaks in his person, saying: I have eaten the honeycomb with my honey; eat, friends, and be drunk, neighbours (Song 5:1). Because of this prophecy, then, and to make his true body manifest, the Lord ate and drank after the resurrection, as blessed Peter the apostle proves, saying: But he was made manifest to us, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead (Acts 10:40-41). For us, then, after the resurrection there will be the food of the Word, and the vision of God, and his praises, and alleluia, and those things which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have they entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love him (1 Cor. 2:9). We shall not, then, have to eat and drink after the resurrection, nor are incorrupt and immortal bodies to be sustained by earthly nourishment; otherwise, where there is food, there follow also diseases, and the other things which we suffer in this world.

CHAPTER XXIX. — Just as, then, the Lord took up true flesh, and truly suffered, and truly rose, and truly after the resurrection showed his hands and side to the disciples (John 20:20; Luke 24:40), so too he truly ate, truly walked with feet, and spoke with a true tongue with all the apostles and with Cleopas, and reclined with them at supper on a true couch, and with true hands took bread and blessed and broke [it] and held [it] out to them. But that he suddenly vanished from their eyes was [a work] of divine power, not of a shadow or a phantom: otherwise, even before the passion, when they had seized him and led him out of Nazareth to throw him down from the brow of the hill (Luke 4:29) on which their city was set, he passed through the midst of them, that is, he slipped from their hands. Or did he not have flesh, who made a whip of cord and drove all his enemies and persecutors out of the temple (John 2:15)? where the whole power of his divinity shone forth. But that after the resurrection he came in to the disciples when the doors were shut was of the same power as his vanishing from their eyes. For men of this world say that Apollonius the magician, when he was standing before the emperor Domitian in the council chamber, suddenly disappeared (Philostratus, book 8, ch. 5; Lactantius, Institutes, book 5, ch. 3). We have said this, however, not to compare a magician filled with a demon to the Lord Christ, but to refute the madness of the heretics. What, then, is permitted to a magician, if indeed it is true, is it not permitted to the Lord? Lynceus, as the stories relate, saw through a wall (Pliny, Natural History, book 28, ch. 8): could the Lord not enter through shut doors unless he were a phantom? he who certainly even before the resurrection walked on the sea with a suspended step (Matt. 14:25), and granted this very thing to the apostle Peter, who, when he was walking on the waters by faith, afterwards began through unbelief to sink, had not the right hand of the Lord quickly held him (Jerome on Isaiah, near the end; also on Matthew ch. 24). Eagles and vultures perceive corpses across the sea: will the Saviour not see his apostles unless he has opened the doors? Finally, I should like you to tell me which is greater, to weigh so great a mass of earth with three fingers (Isa. 40:12) and to be poised upon the unstable waters, or for God to pass through a closed created thing? You attribute what is greater to the Creator, and you cavil at what is less. The apostle Peter, as has already been said, walked on the waters (Matt. 14:29), and the soft wave would not have given way to his heavy and solid body, had he not doubted a little: and do you cavil at God, why he came in through shut doors? Peter's faith, then, doubted a little, and at once the body recognised its own nature; so that we might know that it was not the body that walked on the waters, but faith.

CHAPTER XXX. Do not, by your own judgement, either equate the power of the Lord with the tricks of magicians or make it inferior to them, so that it should seem to have been what it was not, so that he should be thought to have eaten without teeth, broken bread without hands, walked without feet, spoken without tongue or head, shown his side without a body. And how, he says, did they not recognise him on the road, if he had the same body which he had before? You are wrong, and very wrong, you who do not hear the Evangelist saying: For their eyes were held, so that they should not recognise him; and a little after: Their eyes, he says, were opened, and they recognised him (Luke 24:16, 31). Are you so foolish as to say that he was one person when he was recognised, and another when he was not recognised? Surely he was one and the same. Recognising and not recognising, then, belonged to the eyes of those who saw, not to him who was seen, so that the prophecy of holy Jeremiah might be fulfilled, in which he says: Why will you be like a settler in the land, and like a traveller turning aside to stay (Jer. 14:8)? Finally, so that you may know that the error which was at work lay not in the Lord's body but in eyes that were closed: Their eyes were opened (John 20:16), and at once they recognised him. For Mary Magdalene too, as long as she was seeking the living among the dead, did not recognise Jesus; but when she recognised him, she at once confesses him Lord. Again, when all the disciples were together in the boat, Jesus was standing on the shore (John 21:4); and while the others did not recognise him, John recognised him first and said: It is the Lord. It was indeed fitting, and quite appropriate, that virginity should be the first to recognise the virginal body. He was the same, then, and yet was not seen as the same by all.

CHAPTER XXXI. And immediately adding to this, the Evangelist says: And no one dared to ask him any more: Who are you (John 21:12)? For as they ate and drank with him alike, they saw a true man and God; not, however, as though one were God and another man, but [they saw that] the Son of God and the Son of man were one and the same; for he was recognised as man and adored as God, fulfilling what the Lord himself had prayed for them, saying to the Father: And this is eternal life, that they may know you, the one and true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent (John 17:3). It is fitting, then, and entirely fitting, that the flesh of the man in which God deigned to dwell should be brought into heaven; nor can it seem that the man was made an inhabitant of heaven beyond his desert, whose sheath the Spirit, who is God, did not disdain. It was just, therefore, that the body in which God, by dwelling there, deigned to visit the earth, through which he was made a sharer in our nature, he should lead to immortality and set in the heavenly places. Where, then, should God's dwelling be, if not in the kingdom of God? And where is the kingdom of God, if not in the heavens, where we too shall all be, by his gift and help, when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality (1 Cor. 15:53); so that all flesh may see the salvation of God (Isa. 40:5), and know that he is the redeemer and saviour who wrestled with Jacob (Gen. 32:24), who was strength and helper to Jacob himself, who, overcome in his voluntary passion, which that wrestling prefigured, blessed those who crucified him and prayed for them, saying: Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do (Luke 23:34), confirming also what he had foretold through David: While those who ate my flesh drew near to me, I prayed (Ps. 108:4). It is the flesh of the Word, then, not the Word, that is eaten: the flesh is consumed, not God, who is spirit. You, he says, persecuting me, scourged me, you spat in my face, you crucified me: yet I call you to repentance: For I do not desire the death of the sinner, but only that he should turn back and live (Ezek. 18:32). That this is so the blessed Apostle proves, saying: And you, though you were once estranged and enemies in the mind of your flesh in evil works, he has reconciled in the body of his flesh through death (Col. 1:21-22).

CHAPTER XXXII. But as for what they object, that the Apostle said: Those who are in the flesh cannot please God (Rom. 8:8): this was said, not so that the nature of the flesh should be condemned, whose maker is God, and in which very many of the saints have pleased God and reign with Christ, but so that the mind and the works of the flesh should be repudiated (Tertullian, On the Resurrection of the Flesh, ch. 46). When, then, the clay of our flesh, as has already been said, has flown to heaven on spiritual wings, carried up by angels, there it has the true and peace-bringing pledge of its salvation for ever, to whom we shall be caught up in the clouds, to meet Christ in the air (1 Thess. 4:16), as the prophet Isaiah testifies, saying: They will be lifted upon shoulders, and carried to their places (Isa. 66:12); and again: Who are these who fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows (Isa. 60:8)? that is, to the mansions of their merits, of which the Lord says: There are many mansions with my Father (John 14:2); and again: And they will bring all your brothers from all the nations to Jerusalem, on horses and mules and in chariots and carriages and litters, says the Lord God (Isa. 66:20). Lest it should perhaps seem doubtful to anyone that a man placed in this body can fly through the air, the same Apostle confirms it, saying: By faith Enoch was taken up, so that he should not see death (Heb. 11:5); for Elijah too, placed in this body, in which he is to this day, was caught up as if to heaven in a fiery chariot, that is, carried up by angels, who are spirits and a flame of fire, who do his will (4 Kgs. 2:11); and the prophet Habakkuk was led by an angel from Judaea into Chaldaea and brought back in a moment of time (Dan. 14:35); and the apostle Paul himself was caught up to the third heaven (2 Cor. 12:2), and into paradise, and was brought back from there into the world. And so that it may shine out more plainly that these vehicles of the saints are spirits, that is, the angels of God, the example of holy Philip, one of the seven, teaches us, whom the Spirit of the Lord caught away from Gaza and suddenly set down at Azotus (Acts 8:39-40). Let these things, examined in some detail and, as it were, limb by limb and joint by joint, as far as the Lord has deigned to help my purpose, suffice as said. Yet lest we seem to have left anything out, they must be proved by the words of our Lord and Saviour himself; for he says, when he was speaking of the field and the wheat and the darnel: For at the consummation of the age my Father will send angels, who will separate the darnel (Matt. 13:41), that is, sinners, from the wheat, that is, from the righteous. These are the angels who carried Lazarus, proved in the struggle of poverty and sickness together, into the bosom and rest of Abraham (Luke 16:22).

CHAPTER XXXIII. Truly, as it is written: I have proved you in the furnace of poverty (Isa. 48:10). Men are proved, then, in different ways: one through want and bodily sickness, another through riches and bodily health. Yet none of these things are either the highest goods or the highest evils; for the highest evil is eternal death, and the highest good is eternal life. All these things, then, which the life of mortals holds are intermediate; for in both there is temptation: for many whom neither want nor sickness broke, health has broken, and riches destroy. This the most wise Solomon confirms, saying to the Lord: Give me neither riches nor poverty, but grant only what is necessary for my living (Prov. 30:8); that is, lest he should either be exalted in the former, or, brought into the latter, perjure himself or blaspheme. And that these things which we have called intermediate are foreign to us, the Lord confirms, saying: If you have not been faithful in what is another's, who will give you what is your own (Ambrose, On Luke bk. 7, near the end; ibid., bk. 8, n. 85)? Riches, then, are foreign to us, because they are outside our nature; for they are neither born with us nor pass away with us. And so, knowing this, let us not serve what is foreign, we who ought to have no God but Christ. We are guests, then, of our own possessions; for whatever is of the world remains in the world: and whatever we acquire for heirs, we lose for ourselves; for we carry nothing with us but either good or evil works. Riches, then, are not evil, but they are evil to those who use them evilly; for the good things which God made are very good. And therefore the philosophers of this world call nothing the highest good but peace, honour and virtue; and they set down nothing as the highest evil but malice, dishonour, avarice and baseness. The promise and reward of all good things, then, is eternal life: and the threat and requital of all evil things is the second death.

CHAPTER 34. — Although these things may seem to have been said as a digression, they are nevertheless necessary and useful to us: and so we must now return to our order. When, then, the clay of our flesh, as has already been said, has been fired into earthenware, so that what was formerly pressed down to the earth by a heavy weight may, having received the wings of spiritual grace, fly up to heaven borne by the angels, there it has the true and peaceful pledge of its salvation for ever. What could be found more true, more evident, more clear? Yet lest we seem to have left anything out, take the fullest and firmest token of this hope of ours: that bird of the East called the phoenix, unique, famous for its singularity and marvellous for its posterity, which, willingly giving itself burial, departing and succeeding itself by a natural end, is again a phoenix, is again the same, and not another (Tertullian, On the Resurrection of the Flesh ch. 13; author of the Apostolic Constitutions bk. 5, ch. 6; Cyril, Catechesis 18; Lactantius, Ambrose and others). As a proof of this, for the firmness of our hope, the Holy Spirit too, who is God, has set it down in the holy Scriptures, saying: And they shall flourish like the phoenix, that is, they shall flourish out of death, out of their own burial, as the phoenix will rise again from its dust. If, then, the flesh of a bird rises again from its ashes, will the flesh of man not rise again from its ashes? And where is that which the Lord Christ declared, that we are better than many sparrows? Where too is that which he promised us through the Prophet, saying: Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle's (see Rabbi Kimhi and other interpreters on this place; also Peter Damian, Opusc. 52, ch. 23; Albert the Great, On Animals bk. 23; Gesner, Aldrovandi and others)? They report that the nature of this bird is as follows: when it has come to extreme old age, it is said to soar so long into the air that it reaches the clouds and the fire; and touched by that fire, it soon throws itself headlong into a most hidden spring, plunges three times, and is at once restored to the strength and beauty of its former youth. That this will be so for us the blessed Apostle promised, saying: The fire will test what sort of work each one's is. For various birds swallow the grape, the olive and other fruits; and after much heat, passing their seeds through their droppings, vines grow again, trees grow again. If, then, birds do this for your sake at God's command, will God not do it with you, for the sake of faith and of his own reward? Believe me that he will do it, for the sake of his promise; for when we were once nothing, we were made at the command of that very Lord of all creatures. He, then, who made out of nothing what was not, will be able to make again what he had before made out of nothing.

CHAPTER 35. — For if the flesh of man, as the blind heretics falsely claim, will not rise again, how does Isaiah, full of the Spirit of God, who is to be called not so much a prophet as an evangelist, say: All flesh shall come which is to worship in the sight of the Lord, in Jerusalem, to see the corpses of the dead men who have transgressed against God (that is, either the Jews, or the impious, or sinners); their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched (Jerome on the last chapter of Isaiah). Many would have this worm or fire understood as the conscience of sinners, which torments those placed in punishment, because through their own fault and sin they have lacked so great a good, according to what is written: Walk in the light of your fire, and in the flame which you have kindled for yourselves (Isa. 50:11); and again: As the moth [eats] a garment and the worm wood, so grief tortures the heart of a man (Prov. 25:20). For just as gladness of mind sometimes soothes the pains of the body, so pain of mind weighs down and tortures the body, as the prophet says: A rejoicing mind makes a flourishing age; a sad spirit dries up the bones (Prov. 17:22). If, then, it happens that sickness of mind is added to sickness of body, the infirmity is doubled. These things, however, are said in such a way that it is not denied that the punishments of transgressors and of those who deny God are eternal, as Scripture says: The Lord almighty will take vengeance on them on the day of judgment, to put fire and worms into their flesh; and they shall be burned, so that they feel it for ever (Judith 16:20-21). That this will be so our Lord and Saviour confirms, saying: And all shall rise from the dust of the earth, those who have done good, into the resurrection of judgment (John 5:29); and again: Go into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels (Matt. 25:41); and again it is said of him who had no wedding garment: Take him, and with his hands and feet bound, cast him into the outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth (ibid. 22:13). Since, then, hands, and feet, and weeping, and outer darkness, which pertains to the eyes, and gnashing of teeth are most truly declared by the Lord [to be] in the flesh at the future resurrection, I wonder at certain heretics who try to introduce an airy body, to be gradually dissolved into thin air after the resurrection. Just as, then, the saint is the garment of God and is clothed with the tunic of salvation and gladness, so on the contrary the sinner, who bears the image of the old and earthly man, deserves to hear: Behold, all of you, like a garment, the moth will devour you (Isa. 51:8). The diversity of characters, then, is signified in the holy Scriptures by various names. Just as, then, the diversity of trees and of musical instruments in the divine Scriptures signifies the diversity of spiritual grace, so too the diversity of wild beasts and serpents signifies the diversity of sins. These diverse kinds of musical instruments, however, the God of majesty willed to be named and used in the divine books for this reason: that, drawing the people of the Jews away from carnal sacrifices, he might invite them to spiritual and praiseworthy offerings.

But now let what has been said suffice; although, given the greatness of the matter, nothing can ever be said sufficiently about the causes and things named above. And so, holy, venerable, perfect and inseparable Trinity, who are worshipped and adored by us with whole faith, yours is this work, which I, with your help and illumination, have excerpted for my own edification from the books of the Fathers, your servants; and may your perfection be to the glory and praise of your name through all ages of ages. Amen.
